# Is Timing Set Wrong If TDC Doesn't Have All Valves Closed?

When you rebuild an engine or replace a timing chain, the goal is synchronization: ensuring the camshaft lobes align perfectly with the crankshaft so that intake and exhaust valves close precisely at Top Dead Center (TDC). Ideally, when a cylinder is at TDC on its compression stroke, both valves should be fully seated. However, in a V6 configuration like the one described, finding asymmetry between the left and right bank lobes immediately raises red flags about timing alignment or camshaft design.

The core issue here isn't just visual inspection; it's the physical reality of valve overlap and lift profiles. In any four-stroke engine, the camshaft rotates at exactly half the speed of the crankshaft. If you look at a single cylinder in isolation, the cam lobe for that specific cylinder will be at its highest point (maximum lift) when the corresponding crank pin is at 180 degrees from TDC. At true TDC on the compression stroke, the valve should be closing or just beginning to open if overlap exists.

However, the scenario you describedâwhere one bank's lobes are not symmetrical and allow blow-through while the other creates resistanceâis a classic symptom of incorrect timing belt/chain installation or a camshaft that is not level with the crankshaft. When installing a timing kit, mechanics often align the marks on the crank pulley and the cam sprockets. If these marks are aligned but the engine hasn't been rotated to true TDC for verification, you might assume everything is correct. But visual alignment of sprocket marks does not guarantee that all valves are closed simultaneously across all cylinders in a V-configuration.

Consider the mechanics of the blowdown test. When you introduce air into a cylinder at TDC on the compression stroke, you are testing the integrity of the seal created by the piston ring and the valve seats. If air blows through freely, it means either the intake or exhaust valve is not seated. In your case, the left bank allows air to escape, suggesting that when the crank is at the mark, the camshaft is still rotating slightly past the point where the valves should be closed, or the camshaft timing is retarded relative to the crank.

The visual difference between symmetrical and asymmetrical lobes in your photos provides a strong diagnostic clue. If the lobes appear "symmetrical" on the right bank but not the left, it implies that the camshafts might be twisted relative to each other or that the timing marks were misinterpreted during assembly. In many V6 engines, the cam sprocket has multiple alignment holes. Choosing the wrong hole can result in a timing offset of several degrees. This offset is often invisible until you rotate the engine by hand and inspect the valve clearances or perform a leakdown test.

There is a specific pitfall to avoid when diagnosing this: assuming that TDC marks on the outer cover are absolute. These marks indicate crankshaft position, but they do not account for cam rotation phase. If the engine was assembled without rotating it past Top Dead Center to verify valve closure, or if the camshafts were installed with a slight twist, the timing will be "set" visually but mechanically incorrect.

To resolve this, you must physically rotate the crankshaft until each cylinder hits true TDC on the compression stroke. At this point, inspect the cam lobes. If the lobes are not symmetrical in their lift profile relative to the valve position, or if air leaks through, the timing is incorrect. The only way to achieve perfect synchronization where all valves close at the appropriate moments is to ensure the timing marks align exactly as per the manufacturer's specification and then verify by hand-rotating the engine to TDC on every cylinder.

If you are working with a complex multi-valve V6, relying solely on visual marks can be misleading. The trade-off between ease of installation and mechanical accuracy often leads to these errors. Always rotate the engine to TDC before final tightening of the timing belt tensioner or chain guides to ensure the camshaft has settled into its correct position relative to the crankshaft. If the leakdown test fails on one bank but not the other, the fix is almost certainly a re-installation of the timing components with strict adherence to the alignment marks and a final verification step at true TDC.
